newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Postal Service asks one-cent stamp increase.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Postal Service asks one-cent stamp increase.

text.p: The U.S. Postal Service Board of Governors Tuesday voted to request a penny increase for the price of a first-class stamp, bringing the cost of mailing a letter to 33 cents.

For the first time, the group also proposed a decrease in mail rates, requesting a two-cent drop in the price to send mail easily handled by machines, including bill payments and and metered reply envelopes. Customers would use prepaid 30-cent envelopes obtained from participating companies.
The proposals, which must be approved by the independent Postal Rate Commission, will not take effect sooner than May 1998. Rates were last raised in January 1995.
"Today, a penny doesn't go very far," Postal Service Board of Governors chairman Tirso Del Junco said. "But a penny per stamp is all we need."

The one-cent increase would be the smallest rise in first-class stamp prices ever and is less than one-third the rate of inflation, the Postal Service said. It said the average household would pay about 20 cents more per month for mail under the proposals.
The board of governors also is proposing increases in rates for other classes of mail including priority packages, local newspapers, magazines and catalogues.

The Postal Service is expected to bring in an additional $2.4 billion a year if the proposals are enacted. A spokesman said another increase is not expected until the year 2000 if the hike is approved.

The rate proposals come after the post office has posted profits of more than $1 billion in the last two years. However, a spokesman said the Postal Service is proposing the penny increase as a pre-emptive strike against increasing costs.
If the rate hike is not approved, the Postal Service expects to lose $1.4 billion in 1998 and $2.5 billion in 1999.
Several organisations were quick to criticise the board's proposal to hike rates, saying the Postal Service needs to improve quality of service before it raises more money.

"With a record of mishandling the mail, misspending the stamp money and misleading the American public, the Postal Service has made it clear it cannot and should not be trusted with any more of our money until much-needed and long-overdue reforms are in place," National Minority Business Council President and CEO John Robinson said in a statement.
The Postal Rate Commission has 10 months to make a decision.
